**Date:** Thursday

We've reached the point in our capacity planning where the easy answer and the right answer have diverged, and I want to lay out the reasoning before we commit either way. The question on the table is whether we should purchase additional local inference hardware or invest the next quarter in raising utilisation of the fleet we already own. My recommendation, stated up front, is that we spend the next eight to ten weeks on utilisation work before buying anything, with a small, pre-approved budget reserved for hardware if that work stalls.

The case for buying is straightforward and not wrong. Our p95 latency on batch inference has crept up over the last two months, and the team feels it. Queues form during the afternoon peak, and a couple of promising experiments were shelved simply because nobody wanted to wait three hours for a training run. There's a real opportunity cost there: every delayed experiment is a decision we didn't get to make, and sometimes the value of an answer decays quickly. Hardware is also, in one sense, the most reversible option available to us — accelerators hold resale value reasonably well, and if demand shifts we can sell capacity we no longer need. Buying is fast, it's familiar, and it makes the problem disappear for a while.

But that last clause is the tell. Buying makes the problem disappear *for a while*. Our current fleet runs at roughly 35–40% average utilisation, which is not unusual for on-premise GPU deployments, but it does mean that for most hours of the day we own expensive silicon that is mostly idle. The peak problem is a scheduling problem as much as a capacity problem. Our batch jobs and our interactive workloads compete for the same nodes with no real preemption, our longest-running jobs hog memory they no longer need, and we have no mechanism for consolidating small jobs onto partially-used cards. If we buy more hardware without fixing any of that, we will simply reproduce the same 35% utilisation on a larger fleet, at a larger cost, and we'll be having this same conversation in a year with a bigger number attached.

The cost asymmetry matters too. Utilisation work — a proper scheduler, memory-aware queueing, better job binning, maybe MIG partitioning on the cards that support it — costs engineering time, which is real but bounded, and it's work that compounds: whatever we build makes every future hardware purchase smaller and cheaper. Buying hardware costs capital immediately, plus ongoing power, cooling, and rack space, and it commits us to a depreciation schedule on equipment whose useful life is uncertain. There's also a subtler opportunity cost: the engineering time we'd spend racking and integrating new machines is time not spent on the product work that presumably justifies the fleet's existence.

On reliability, the picture is mixed and worth being honest about. More hardware does give us redundancy; right now, the failure of one particular node takes a meaningful slice of our capacity with it, and that's a genuine argument for a second purchase eventually. But better scheduling also improves reliability in the sense that matters most to users — jobs fail less often when they're not contending for oversubscribed resources, and we can build in headroom policies deliberately rather than accidentally. I'd rather have deliberate headroom than accidental surplus.

The reversibility argument, examined more carefully, cuts both ways. Hardware is reversible in the sense that it can be resold; the utilisation work is reversible in the sense that it changes nothing about our option to buy later. But the *decision to buy now* forecloses less than it appears: the money spent is gone, and the fleet's fixed costs continue regardless of whether we needed it. Deferring the purchase keeps every option open, including the option to buy, and costs us only time.

That time is the real risk, and I want to acknowledge it plainly. If our utilisation work slips, or if it turns out our peak demand is genuinely inelastic — that we truly need more concurrent capacity at 2pm and no scheduler can conjure it — then we will have spent two months to arrive where we started, plus two months of degraded latency. That's why I'm proposing a time-boxed effort with a concrete target: lift average utilisation above 55% and bring p95 batch latency under our agreed threshold. If we hit it, we likely defer purchase by at least two quarters. If we miss it, we buy, with better data about what we actually need and, probably, a smaller purchase than we'd have made today.

The recommendation, then: schedule the utilisation work now, define the success metrics this week, and pre-authorise the hardware budget so that a failed experiment converts quickly into a purchase rather than into another round of debate. We are not choosing between spending and saving; we are choosing the order in which we spend, and the order matters more than it first appears.

# Memo: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Capacity planning for the next two quarters

## The situation

We're at the point where our inference cluster is running hot. Peak-hour queue times have crept from seconds to minutes, and two of our four A100 nodes are now effectively pinned during business hours. The obvious question on the table is whether we should purchase additional hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the framing matters more than the answer itself.

## The case for buying

Buying hardware is the straightforward fix. It removes the constraint immediately, it's easy to reason about, and it gives us headroom for the experimental work we keep deferring — the fine-tuning runs, the internal tooling prototypes, the model evaluations that currently get scheduled into weekend windows nobody loves. There's also a reliability argument: right now we have no meaningful failure tolerance. If a node goes down during peak load, we degrade user-facing performance immediately. A fifth node would give us genuine redundancy rather than a cluster that only works when everything works.

But the purchase is expensive in more ways than the invoice. Beyond the capital cost, which is substantial at current prices, we'd be taking on power, cooling, and maintenance commitments that persist whether or not we use the capacity. And hardware depreciates fast in this market — the card that looks like a good buy today may be badly outclassed in eighteen months. That's a real risk of locking capital into an asset that loses value quickly.

## The case for utilisation work

The alternative is to look hard at our own numbers first. When I sampled our scheduling logs last month, average GPU utilisation during "peak" hours was around 60 percent, which is another way of saying that 40 percent of our most expensive resource is idle even when we feel constrained. Batch sizes are conservative, several services run with generous memory reservations they rarely touch, and our autoscaling policy was written before we understood our own traffic patterns. There's also a batch workload — the embedding refresh jobs — that runs interactively alongside inference and could move to off-peak windows with modest effort.

The honest counterargument is that utilisation work is engineering time, and engineering time is not free. It's an opportunity cost: the two or three engineer-weeks this would consume are weeks not spent on product work. There's also a ceiling. Even executed perfectly, optimisation buys us maybe 30 to 40 percent more effective capacity, and if our workload keeps growing the way it has, we'll hit that ceiling within a year or so. Optimisation delays the purchase; it doesn't eliminate it.

## How I'm weighing it

The decisive factor for me is reversibility. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale — once we've spent the capital, that money is gone, and if demand shifts or a better generation of hardware arrives, we're stuck. Utilisation work, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible and compounding: better batching, right-sized reservations, and smarter scheduling pay off regardless of what hardware we eventually own, and the skills and tooling transfer to whatever we buy later. When one option preserves optionality and the other forecloses it, and both address the near-term problem, the reversible one should usually win.

Latency is the one place where buying has a genuine edge. Some of our queue-time pain is structural — certain requests simply need more compute than our current nodes can give in one pass, and no amount of scheduling cleverness fixes that. If user-facing latency degrades much further, that argument gets stronger and the calculus shifts.

Meanwhile, the utilisation gap is essentially free capacity. Right now, an interactive request rarely waits because the fleet is half-idle; if we pack the machines tighter, p99 latency will degrade unless we're careful about isolation and preemption. This is a real cost, not a hand-wave. But the current setup buys that low latency at an extravagant price, and much of our interactive traffic is tolerant of modest queueing — our own measurements show most requests complete well inside the latency budget even under simulated 70% load. The jobs that genuinely need guaranteed headroom are few enough that we can pin them to dedicated capacity rather than keeping the whole fleet underloaded.

Reliability cuts both ways, and it's worth saying so plainly. More hardware means more components, more failure modes, and more maintenance surface — a bigger fleet is not automatically a more reliable one. On the other hand, running hotter reduces our slack to absorb failures: if a node dies at 75% utilisation, the displaced work has somewhere to go but the margin is thinner. I think this concern is manageable — our failure domain is a single node, and we can hold a deliberate 15–20% buffer for exactly this purpose — but it's the strongest argument on the buy side and we shouldn't pretend otherwise.

The skills and tooling we build doing it will pay off regardless of what hardware we eventually own, and it will make any future purchase smarter, because we'll know our true demand curve rather than our peak anxiety.

Better utilisation is the opposite — it's a set of software changes we can tune, unwind, or supersede as our workload evolves. We have not attempted any of this. Our serving stack is essentially the naive baseline.

## The case for buying

The vendor quote for four additional cards is roughly £58k including networking, rackspace, and a support contract. That would take peak capacity from saturated to comfortable and buy us perhaps 18 months of headroom at current growth rates. Second, buying now removes the pressure to fix our scheduling, which means we'd be paying to perpetuate a 38%-utilisation baseline. Third, there's an opportunity cost: that £58k is roughly one engineer-year, and the same money spent on a focused two-month effort on our serving layer would likely deliver more usable capacity than the hardware would.
